cardiac_monitoring.impression: Sinus rhythm throughout. No sustained arrhythmia, pause or AV block.

findings: Structurally normal heart. No intracardiac thrombus or vegetation. No pericardial effusion.

pre_post_comparison.Timed Up and Go: baseline 27 s; 2 hours 23 s (15% faster); 24 hours 21 s (22% faster)

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Evans index 0.33, callosal angle 86 degrees, temporal horn enlargement, DESH absent, Fazekas 1, patent aqueduct and no obstructing lesion; symmetric pallidal T1 hyperintensity; normal cerebellar volume
action_criteria.label: Brain MRI for the iNPH markers and to exclude an obstructing lesion
action_criteria.rationale: After meningitis the MRI must show a communicating pattern without obstruction before CSF is removed, and it also addresses the liver-related and alcohol-related mimics.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Platelets 88 x10^9/L and INR 1.4, both within the usual lumbar puncture thresholds; ammonia normal
action_criteria.label: Platelet count and coagulation before the lumbar tap in cirrhosis
action_criteria.rationale: Cirrhosis with varices makes thrombocytopenia and a raised INR likely, and both decide whether the tap can proceed safely.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: TUG 27 s, 10-m walk 21 s in 24 steps, 180-degree turn in 6 steps, with a wide-based magnetic gait and impaired postural reflexes
action_criteria.label: Baseline timed gait assessment before the tap
action_criteria.rationale: The falls and shuffling gait need timed baseline values before CSF removal, or the tap response cannot be measured.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: MoCA 21/30 with executive, attention and free-recall deficits and cueing benefit
action_criteria.label: Bedside cognitive screen (MoCA)
action_criteria.rationale: A baseline MoCA documents the executive and retrieval profile and gives a second measure to repeat after the tap.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Opening pressure 16 cmH2O with normal cells, protein and glucose; after 40 mL, TUG 27 to 23 s at 2 hours and 21 s at 24 hours (22%), 10-m walk 21 to 17 s, MoCA 21 to 22
action_criteria.label: CSF tap test with opening pressure
action_criteria.rationale: Normal opening pressure and content confirm a normal-pressure communicating hydrocephalus long after the meningitis, and the tap response predicts shunt benefit.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: TUG 23 s at 2 hours and 21 s at 24 hours (22% faster), 10-m walk 17 s in 20 steps, MoCA 22/30
action_criteria.label: Post-tap timed gait reassessment
action_criteria.rationale: Repeating the same timed measures at 2 and 24 hours turns the CSF removal into a test of shunt responsiveness.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not perform large-volume lumbar puncture before MRI excludes mass effect or obstructive hydrocephalus

Do not diagnose iNPH from ventriculomegaly alone: the diagnosis needs the clinical syndrome (gait disturbance with cognitive or urinary symptoms) and supportive imaging, with no other cause explaining them [Relkin_2005]
Do not attribute the syndrome to hepatic encephalopathy or escalate its treatment without asterixis, raised ammonia or a fluctuating course
Do not transfuse platelets or plasma before the lumbar tap: platelets 88 x10^9/L and INR 1.4 are within the usual thresholds (platelets 50 x10^9/L or more, INR 1.5 or less)
required_recommendations: Refer to neurosurgery for CSF shunting with a programmable valve for secondary normal pressure hydrocephalus after pneumococcal meningitis, on the basis of the tap-test improvement of 22% in TUG at 24 hours, the supportive MRI (Evans index 0.33, callosal angle 86 degrees) and normal-pressure CSF, with hepatology input on perioperative coagulation [Nakajima_2021]
Continue lactulose (titrated to 2 to 3 soft stools a day) and rifaximin 550 mg twice daily unchanged as secondary prophylaxis of hepatic encephalopathy
Falls-prevention measures (physiotherapy, home assessment, walking aid) while awaiting surgery

avoided_actions.rationale: With no asterixis, normal ammonia and no fluctuation, an EEG for encephalopathy adds nothing to a gait-predominant syndrome.
No syncope or palpitations are reported; the falls are gait falls, not blackouts.
No cardioembolic or syncopal question exists in this case.
MRI is available and measures the ventricles, temporal horns and callosal angle better than CT.
Rhythm monitoring has no role without syncope or palpitations.
Molecular or advanced imaging does not change the decision, which rests on MRI and the tap test; no neurodegenerative copathology is in question.
A full neuropsychological battery is not needed for the iNPH decision; the bedside screen and timed gait measures are.
The meningitis was 8 years ago with full recovery and the CSF cell count is normal, so infectious, inflammatory and prion CSF assays have no indication.

accepted: Secondary normal pressure hydrocephalus, post-meningitic arachnoiditis

differential.diagnosis: Covert hepatic encephalopathy or acquired hepatocerebral degeneration
differential.key_features: Cirrhosis and pallidal T1 hyperintensity raise it, but there is no asterixis, the ammonia is normal on prophylaxis, the course does not fluctuate and the gait improved after CSF removal.
The imaging and tap response are the same, but a documented antecedent (pneumococcal meningitis) makes the hydrocephalus secondary.
Past heavy drinking and a wide-based gait raise it, but he has been abstinent 5 years, has no truncal ataxia and the cerebellar volume is normal on MRI.

differential.diagnosis: Vascular cognitive impairment / subcortical ischaemic small-vessel disease
differential.key_features: White matter change is only Fazekas 1, without lacunes, and cannot explain the ventriculomegaly or the tap response.
No rest tremor, asymmetric rigidity or upper limb bradykinesia; the gait disorder is lower-body and responded to CSF removal.

differential.diagnosis: Cerebral atrophy with secondary ex-vacuo ventriculomegaly
differential.key_features: Acute callosal angle and temporal horns enlarged out of proportion to the hippocampi, with an objective tap response, argue against atrophy.

key_clinical_evidence: Communicating hydrocephalus with an identified antecedent (here pneumococcal meningitis 8 years earlier, by post-meningitic arachnoiditis) is secondary normal pressure hydrocephalus, not iNPH; it is investigated and shunted by the same route.

Imaging: Evans index 0.33 with an acute callosal angle (86 degrees) and enlarged temporal horns, no DESH and no obstruction; the pallidal T1 hyperintensity is the manganese deposition common in cirrhosis.

Opening pressure 16 cmH2O with normal CSF content; after 40 mL, TUG improved 22% at 24 hours (27 to 21 s) with a concordant 10-m walk change. A 10% or greater TUG improvement is a commonly used positive criterion; tap-test sensitivity is 26% to 61% and PPV 73% to 100% (Marmarou 2005).
Hepatic encephalopathy is unlikely: no asterixis, normal ammonia, no fluctuation, and a gait-predominant syndrome that responded to CSF removal.
Platelets 88 x10^9/L and INR 1.4 are within the usual thresholds for lumbar puncture (platelets 50 x10^9/L or more, INR 1.5 or less); no transfusion is needed for the tap.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: No asterixis, a normal ammonia and a slowly progressive, gait-predominant syndrome without fluctuation argue against hepatic encephalopathy as the cause.
red_herrings.data_point: Alcohol-related cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B, score 7; one episode of overt hepatic encephalopathy 2 years ago, on lactulose and rifaximin; no ascites; abstinent 5 years)
red_herrings.intended_effect: The syndrome is attributed to hepatic encephalopathy

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Symmetric pallidal T1 hyperintensity is the manganese deposition common in cirrhosis; without parkinsonism or encephalopathy it does not explain the gait disorder.
red_herrings.data_point: Symmetric T1 hyperintensity of the globus pallidus bilaterally
red_herrings.intended_effect: The gait disorder is attributed to acquired hepatocerebral degeneration

sequence_constraints.reason: Brain imaging must exclude a mass or obstructive hydrocephalus before CSF is removed [Relkin_2005]
The baseline gait must be measured before the tap, or the post-tap change cannot be interpreted [Nakajima_2021]

findings.result: Wide-based, shuffling gait with reduced step height and a magnetic quality at gait initiation.
En-bloc turn in 6 steps for 180 degrees, unsteady.
Pull test: three steps of retropulsion, recovers unaided.
Three falls in the past 6 months reported.

clinical_assessment.impression: Slow, wide-based, short-stepped gait with gait-initiation hesitancy, en-bloc turning and impaired postural reflexes.

csf.interpretation: Normal opening pressure and normal CSF cell count, protein and glucose. After removal of 40 mL, TUG changed from 27 s to 23 s at 2 hours and 21 s at 24 hours (22% at 24 hours); 10-m walk 21 s to 17 s at 24 hours; MoCA 21 to 22.

labs.interpretation: Mild anaemia and thrombocytopenia (platelets 88 x10^9/L); INR 1.4; mildly raised bilirubin and low albumin. Normal ammonia, sodium, creatinine, TSH and vitamin B12.

additional_observations: Technique: 3T brain MRI with sagittal T1, axial T2, FLAIR, DWI, SWI and coronal 3D T1 for callosal angle and hippocampi; no contrast.
No restricted diffusion. No microbleeds on SWI. No mass, haemorrhage or extra-axial collection. Basal cisterns patent.
Cerebellar vermis and hemispheres of normal volume.
Hippocampal volumes preserved for age (MTA score 1 bilaterally).

signal_characteristics.description: Enlarged lateral and third ventricles; Evans index 0.33.

findings.location: corpus callosum, coronal plane through the posterior commissure
temporal horns of the lateral ventricles, bilateral

signal_characteristics.description: Temporal horns enlarged bilaterally, out of proportion to hippocampal volume.
High-convexity and medial parietal sulci not effaced; Sylvian fissures not disproportionately enlarged. DESH morphology absent.
Thin periventricular caps and a smooth rim of T2/FLAIR hyperintensity, Fazekas grade 1.
Aqueduct patent with a flow void; fourth ventricle mildly enlarged. No obstructing lesion, mass or aqueductal stenosis.
Symmetric T1 hyperintensity of the globus pallidus bilaterally, without T2 or FLAIR change.

mri.impression: 1. Communicating ventriculomegaly (Evans index 0.33) with an acute callosal angle of 86 degrees, temporal horn enlargement and no obstructing lesion; DESH morphology absent. 2. Symmetric pallidal T1 hyperintensity. 3. Mild periventricular white matter hyperintensity (Fazekas 1).

metadata.difficulty_rationale: 3 required (MRI, baseline gait, CSF tap), 2 recommended (platelets and coagulation, post-tap reassessment) and 1 optional (MoCA) actions; 2 grounded red herrings; 6 differential alternatives.
metadata.difficulty_variant_description: Secondary normal pressure hydrocephalus 8 years after pneumococcal meningitis in alcohol-related cirrhosis: hepatic encephalopathy and pallidal manganese red herrings, and a thrombocytopenia and INR safety question before the tap.
metadata.revision_reason: case-level re-audit of all NPH reviewer requests: the tap report is routed to CSF, timed gait/cognitive assessment is the required pre/post measure, the standalone neuropsychological battery and advanced imaging are removed from gold actions and callable authored follow-ups, laboratories remain optional, unrelated CSF assays are no longer returned for free, and the unsupported universal 20% response threshold is corrected

patient.chief_complaint: Progressive gait disorder with falls, cognitive slowing and urinary incontinence over 10 months

past_medical_history: Alcohol-related cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B, score 7; one episode of overt hepatic encephalopathy 2 years ago, on lactulose and rifaximin; no ascites; abstinent 5 years)
Oesophageal varices on propranolol, no previous bleed
Pneumococcal meningitis 8 years ago, full recovery

social_history.alcohol: Abstinent for 5 years (previously about 8 to 10 drinks a day for 20 years)
social_history.tobacco: Former smoker, quit with alcohol cessation 5 years ago

patient.history_present_illness: A 65-year-old right-handed man with alcohol-related cirrhosis (abstinent 5 years), pneumococcal meningitis 8 years ago from which he recovered fully, and hypertension was admitted for evaluation of progressive neurological deterioration over 10 months, referred by his hepatologist. He has developed a shuffling, wide-based gait with 3 falls in the past 6 months, progressive slowing of thought with memory complaints, and urinary urgency with incontinence. His hepatologist considered recurrent hepatic encephalopathy, but ammonia levels have been normal on lactulose and rifaximin, which he has taken since a single episode of overt hepatic encephalopathy 2 years ago, and his family report no day-to-day fluctuation or sleep inversion. A brain MRI obtained 3 months ago at an outside facility was reported as showing enlarged ventricles; the images are not available.

neurological_exam.additional: No asterixis. Spider angiomata on the upper chest and palmar erythema. No fetor hepaticus, no ascites.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-nose intact. Heel-shin mildly awkward bilaterally. No truncal ataxia when seated.
neurological_exam.gait: Wide-based, shuffling gait with a magnetic quality, reduced step height and en-bloc turns; unsteady on turning.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert, attentive, oriented, slowed responses; formal cognitive screening reported separately.
neurological_exam.motor: Normal strength throughout. Mildly increased tone bilateral lower extremities.
neurological_exam.sensory: Vibration mildly reduced at the ankles; light touch and proprioception preserved.
